snip.t: CT/MR angiography: Is there aortic coarctation or aneurysm? — Narrowing of aortic arch, delayed femoral pulses

Safety: Anticoagulation is generally contraindicated or held in active native-valve infective endocarditis due to the high risk of fatal intracerebral haemorrhage from septic embolic infarctions or ruptured mycotic aneurysms.

Vasculitis is a heterogeneous group of disorders characterised by inflammation of blood vessel walls, leading to vessel wall damage, luminal narrowing or occlusion, aneurysm formation and downstream tissue ischaemia or necrosis.

Understanding that inflammation can begin in any layer but most clinically relevant damage occurs when the media and adventitia are breached, causing aneurysm or rupture, or when the intima thickens, causing stenosis.
Left ventricular aneurysm formation causing persistent ST-segment elevation, chronic heart failure, and systemic thromboembolism.

snip.t: Local extension: Conduction block (new PR prolongation or bundle branch block indicating aortic root extension), perivalvular abscess, fistula, or large false aneurysm.

qs.q: When evaluating the anatomical distribution of saccular (berry) aneurysms in the Circle of Willis, which site is the most frequently affected?
qs.e: The anterior communicating artery is the most common site for saccular aneurysms, accounting for roughly 40% of cases. The middle cerebral artery bifurcation is the second most common site.

qs.q: What is the primary medical intervention used to reduce the risk of coronary artery aneurysms in Kawasaki disease?
qs.e: Administration of IVIG and aspirin significantly reduces the development of coronary artery aneurysms in Kawasaki disease from 25% down to 4-9%. Standard induction cytotoxic drugs are not the primary treatment for this condition.

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman dies suddenly from a subarachnoid hemorrhage caused by a ruptured berry aneurysm. Histological examination of the aneurysm neck typically reveals which structural alteration?
qs.e: Saccular aneurysms characteristically lack a media and the internal elastic lamina at the neck, representing the site of structural weakness. A normal arterial wall contains a robust media and elastic layers rather than total absence.

qs.q: Which of the following locations is the most common site for a saccular aneurysm in the anterior circulation?
qs.e: The anterior communicating artery/ACA junction is the most common site, accounting for 40% of saccular aneurysms. The MCA bifurcation is the second most common at 34%.

qs.q: Which of the following is a recognized risk factor for the development of saccular aneurysms?
qs.e: ADPKD is a known associated condition that increases the risk of saccular aneurysms. Hemophilia is a bleeding disorder, not a vascular wall defect risk factor for aneurysm formation.

qs.q: Why are saccular aneurysms considered to have a developmental origin despite not being present at birth?
o: They result from congenital absence of the external elastic lamina
They arise from persistent embryonic vessels
They are caused by in-utero exposure to teratogens
They develop due to an underlying defect in the vessel wall media
qs.e: Saccular aneurysms develop over time due to an underlying structural defect in the vessel wall media, specifically the absence of smooth muscle and elastic lamina. They are not present at birth.

qs.q: Which of the following is a common site for atherosclerotic (fusiform) aneurysms?
qs.e: Atherosclerotic aneurysms are mostly found in the basilar artery. Saccular aneurysms are more common in the anterior circulation branch points like the ACA and MCA.

qs.q: Which histological finding is characteristic of the wall of an unruptured saccular aneurysm?
o: Thickened muscular media with intact elastic lamina
Thickened hyalinised intima and adventitia only
Deposition of beta-amyloid in the media
qs.e: The wall of a saccular aneurysm consists of a thickened hyalinised intima and adventitia, lacking the smooth muscle and elastic lamina found in normal arteries. Beta-amyloid is seen in CAA.

ai.title: Aneurysm
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: An aneurysm is a focal dilatation of a blood vessel wall due to structural weakness. In low‑resource settings the most common causes are infectious (tuberculous, syphilitic, mycotic) and inflammatory (vasculitis, rheumatic disease).

sections.p: An aneurysm is a localized, permanent dilation of a vessel exceeding 50% of its normal diameter. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion and imaging; when CT/MRI are unavailable, bedside ultrasound or plain radiographs can suggest a large mass or pulsatile swelling.

t.b: Is there a pulsatile, anechoic cavity? – Aaneurysm appears as a saccular or fusiform echo‑free space with blood flow on Doppler.
Does a soft‑tissue mass have a calcified rim? – Calcification suggests chronic aneurysm; absence does not rule out acute disease.

sections.p: Aneurysms are staged by size, growth rate and risk of rupture. The Society for Vascular Surgery (SVS) grading classifies abdominal aortic aneurysms: I (<5.5 cm), II (5.5–6.5 cm), III (>6.5 cm).
b: Size >5.5 cm or rapid growth >0.5 cm/year

sections.p: In East Africa the leading causes are infectious and inflammatory. The table lists common etiologies in order of likelihood.
b: Infectious: TB, syphilis, HIV‑associated mycotic aneurysm
Inflammatory: Takayasu arteritis, Kawasaki disease, rheumatic heart disease

sections.p: Presentation depends on location. Common features include a pulsatile mass, localized pain, and systemic signs of infection or inflammation.
When advanced imaging is unavailable, use the most accessible tests to rule out rupture and assess size.

t.b: Is the vessel dilated and does it have a thrombus? – Confirms aneurysm and shows intraluminal clot.
Is there leukocytosis or anemia? – Suggests infection or chronic blood loss.
Is inflammation elevated? – Supports vasculitis or infectious etiology.
Are there positive antibodies? – Identifies specific infectious causes.
Is there a calcified rim? – Indicates chronic aneurysm.

sections.p: Urgent care is required if there are signs of rupture or impending rupture.
Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care. Anticoagulation is avoided if infection is present.
b: Penicillin for syphilitic aneurysm (penicillin G 3–4 million IU q4h for 10–14 days)
Surgical repair or endovascular stent graft if size >5.5 cm or symptomatic

sections.p: Regular imaging every 6–12 months for stable aneurysms; control blood pressure, treat infections, and counsel on smoking cessation.
Aneurysm can be mistaken for a tumour, abscess or hematoma.
b: Abscess – usually tender, fluctuating, no pulsation

sections.p: Low‑grade infection may give normal CRP; small aneurysms may be missed on plain X‑ray.
Any sudden change in pain, haemodynamic instability or neurological deficit warrants immediate transfer.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of aortic aneurysm in East Africa?

faq.a: Yes, many are found incidentally on imaging for other reasons.
Only if the aneurysm is >5.5 cm, symptomatic, or rapidly expanding; otherwise surveillance is acceptable.

exam: What is the first investigation you would order for a patient with a pulsatile abdominal mass in a low‑resource setting? — Bedside ultrasound to confirm aneurysm and assess thrombus.
How would you differentiate a mycotic aneurysm from atherosclerotic aneurysm clinically? — Fever, leukocytosis, positive infection serology versus isolated hypertension and smoking history.

A patient with a known abdominal aneurysm presents with sudden severe pain and hypotension. What is your immediate management? — Suspect rupture: stabilize haemodynamics, arrange emergency transfer, avoid anticoagulation.
Why is anticoagulation contraindicated in a mycotic aneurysm? — Risk of haemorrhage from infected vessel wall and septic emboli.
Which drug class is preferred for treating syphilitic aneurysm? — Penicillin G, high‑dose intravenous for 10–14 days.
In a patient with a 6.0 cm abdominal aneurysm and uncontrolled hypertension, what is the next best step? — Tight blood‑pressure control, schedule elective repair, and monitor size every 6 months.
